common_misconceptions.misconception: Students often write that the New Deal ended the Depression. Unemployment did fall sharply but only the war economy from 1941 returned the USA to full employment; the New Deal cushioned suffering and rebuilt confidence rather than fully ending the slump.
common_misconceptions.source: AQA principal examiner commentary on Paper 1 Section A/D extended-response answers; Hodder Education AQA GCSE History America 1920-1973 textbook overview

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students assume the 1920s Boom raised every American's living standard. In fact, farmers, sharecroppers, African-Americans in the South, Native Americans, recent immigrants and many industrial workers were excluded — inequality is a core spec theme.
common_misconceptions.source: AQA subject content for America, 1920-1973 (Part one bullet on inequalities of wealth); Pearson AQA GCSE History America 1920-1973 student book topic-weighting guidance

common_misconceptions.topic: Martin Luther King vs Malcolm X
common_misconceptions.misconception: Students conflate or sharply caricature the two figures, presenting King as purely peaceful and Malcolm X as purely violent. The spec asks students to handle peaceful protest, the Black Power Movement and Civil Rights Acts as connected strands of the same struggle.
common_misconceptions.source: AQA subject content for America, 1920-1973 (Part three bullets on King and Malcolm X); Historical Association Polychronicon 138 on civil rights movement historiography

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students treat the flapper image as proof that all 1920s women were liberated, then jump straight to 1960s feminism. The spec requires students to weigh limited 1920s gains against rural reality, depression-era setbacks, war work and the 1960s/70s women's movement.
common_misconceptions.source: AQA subject content for America, 1920-1973 (Part one position of women, Part three feminist movements)

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students retell the story without explaining why the case mattered — it is named in the spec because it shows the intersection of the Red Scare, immigration restriction and prejudice against Italian-Americans, not just as a famous trial.
common_misconceptions.source: AQA subject content for America, 1920-1973 (Part one — significance of Sacco and Vanzetti)

student_errors_by_question_type.4 marks — Compare Interpretations: Students answer 'why interpretations differ' here instead of 'how they differ'. The 4-mark compare task asks for a clear summary of the contrasting view in each interpretation, supported by short references — not a discussion of authors or purposes.
student_errors_by_question_type.4 marks — Why Interpretations Differ: Students explain how interpretations differ (what each says) instead of why (focus, evidence used, purpose, time of writing). Examiners flag this as a recurring confusion across series.
student_errors_by_question_type.8 marks — Evaluate an Interpretation: Students agree or disagree without rooting their argument in their own contextual knowledge of 1920s-1970s America. The highest-band answers always weave content, provenance and own knowledge together.
student_errors_by_question_type.8 marks — Explain Effects: Students list events that followed (e.g. 'after the Crash, banks closed') without analysing the chain of consequences. Top answers track second- and third-order effects on different groups.
student_errors_by_question_type.12 marks — Bullet-Format Essay: Students cover both bullet points but never reach a substantiated overall judgement, so they cap below the top band. Examiner reports stress that judgements are often asserted at the end with no supporting reasoning.

topic_weighting_notes: Part 1 (Boom) and Part 3 (post-war) carry the heaviest exam weighting — civil rights and the New Deal are recurring 12-mark topics. Allocate 5 lessons to Part 1 (Boom + divided society), 4 to Part 2 (Bust), 5 to Part 3 (post-war).

Within Part 1, treat 'inequalities of wealth' and 'divided society' as equal in weight to the Boom itself. Examiners reward students who can argue both sides — opportunity AND inequality — within a single answer.

Civil rights (Lesson 13) deserves the most depth in Part 3. The spec lists segregation laws, MLK, peaceful protest, Malcolm X, Black Power and the 1964 and 1968 Civil Rights Acts as named content; all must be covered.

The 'Great Society' bullet is dense — Kennedy's New Frontier, Johnson's reforms, NOW, Roe v Wade, the 1972 Equal Rights ruling AND opposition to the ERA all sit in one lesson and need careful sequencing.

Roosevelt's contribution as president' is named explicitly in the spec — practise judgement questions that ask students to weigh his role against structural factors (WWII, the alphabet agencies, opposition).
current_spec_changes: No subject-content changes for the 2026 series — the specification dated 24 September 2019 (version 1.3) remains current; the assessment structure is unchanged.
There is no Historic Environment site for this period study — that requirement applies only to the British depth study options.
pedagogical_notes: EEF guidance on disciplinary literacy applies strongly here: front-load second-order vocabulary (cause, consequence, change, continuity, significance) so students can deploy it in extended responses about the Boom-Bust-Recovery arc.

EEF metacognition guidance — model interpretation questions out loud rather than handing students a checklist. Walk through how you decide what differs and why on a contrasting pair of New Deal interpretations or civil rights accounts.

Cambridge Assessment research highlights comparative judgement as the single hardest skill at GCSE — schedule extra retrieval and worked examples on 12-mark judgement essays comparing factors (e.g. 'How important was Roosevelt himself in delivering recovery?').

When introducing civil rights, sequence the named figures and Acts chronologically (Brown 1954 → Montgomery 1955 → Little Rock 1957 → sit-ins 1960 → Freedom Rides 1961 → Birmingham/March on Washington 1963 → Civil Rights Act 1964 → Selma/Voting Rights 1965 → Black Power → 1968 Act). The narrative structure prevents students from collapsing the decade into a single moment.

Use the inequality framing as a spine across the unit: every lesson in Parts 1 and 3 should explicitly ask 'opportunity for whom, inequality for whom?' — this is the unit title and the principal examiner's preferred analytical lens.
